newsitem.title: USA: ABA ethics panel opposes pay-to-play restriction.
newsitem.headline: ABA ethics panel opposes pay-to-play restriction.

text.p: A key American Bar Association panel voted this weekend to reject a controversial proposal by New York City's bar association designed to restrict pay-to-play practices by bond lawyers, the committee's chairman said.

Lawrence Fox, chairman of ABA's Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility, said in a telephone interview that his 10-member panel's vote to oppose the policy being pushed by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York was unanimous. Fox's panel voted at a meeting in Bermuda.

The New York City bar last year adopted a rule, which it updated recently, that would restrict municipal bond lawyers that solicit or make contributions to muni clients, including some PAC contributions, from engaging in bond business for two years with those governments.
The rule is generally modeled after a standard adopted by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board in 1994 for bond dealers, although the City bar's rule is more restrictive.
ABA delegates are scheduled to vote on whether to adopt the policy at the association's annual meeting this August in San Francisco.

Chairmen of several influential ABA panels have raised serious concerns about the City bar's language, which the administrative board for New York State courts is currently reviewing for possible adoption statewide.
Fox's panel is considered one of the most influential since it is ABA-wide, rather than a committee of a particular ABA section.

"We are as a committee unanimously opposed to the proposal," Fox said, noting that his panel will circulate a "Dear Colleague" letter to other ABA leaders on the issue in the next week. "We will oppose the proposal on the floor of the House," he said, referring to ABA's House of Delegates.
Fox stressed, "We are prepared to have a dialogue with anybody" over the issue. He said the City bar did not seek enough formal input from the association before presenting the resolution.

Fox said he hopes his committee's action this weekend will be "persuasive." It will not be "the first time that ABA's Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility took a position on the floor of the House and lost," he said. "That's happened a number of times. I don't have a good sense of the pulse of the world on this."
Fox said the panel opposes the City bar proposal for several reasons.
"We do not know whether there really is a problem here that should be addressed," he said. Existing ABA model rules of conduct already "capture anything that's illegal," he said.

"We feel very strongly that we should not have special rules for any particular group of lawyers (or) any particular kind of legal work," Fox continued. "We are very much in favor of the model rule approach - that all rules apply to all lawyers in all facets of their conduct."

He added that his panel has "serious" First Amendment questions about the Ciy bar rule. "We are very concerned about taking lawyers out of the political process when others are free to participate," he said.
Fox said the policy, if adopted by ABA, would leave firms with few options. "You wipe out my lawfirm or we drop out of the municipal finance business, one or the other," Fox said.
"That's 250 lawyers here, 250 lawyers there. Before you know it you are up to 10,000, 20,000 50,000 lawyers not allowed to participate in the political process," Fox said.
